nameStory: The Pacific Bleeding Heart gets its dramatic name from its distinctive heart-shaped flowers that appear to have a drop of blood or tear hanging from the bottom, creating the illusion of a 'bleeding' heart. The 'Pacific' part tells you this wildflower originally calls the West Coast home, from the Pacific Northwest down through California.
description: Pacific Bleeding Heart is a delicate woodland perennial that looks like it stepped out of a fairy tale garden. It produces clusters of drooping, heart-shaped flowers in shades of pink, purple, yellow, or cream that dangle gracefully above fern-like, deeply divided leaves. The plant typically grows 1-2 feet tall and spreads by underground rhizomes to form attractive colonies. While native to the Pacific Coast, it's occasionally found in New England gardens and has rarely escaped to the wild.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Heart-shaped flowers about an inch long hang in drooping clusters, with two outer petals forming the 'heart' and inner petals creating a white or pale 'droplet' at the bottom that gives the bleeding effect

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, blue-green leaves are deeply divided into many small segments, creating a delicate, fern-like texture that feels smooth and somewhat succulent to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low mounds or colonies 12-24 inches tall, spreading gradually by underground stems with an overall soft, mounded appearance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, somewhat fleshy stems that break cleanly when snapped and may release a slightly bitter, watery sap

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces narrow, pod-like capsules that split open to release small, shiny black seeds

habitat: In New England, Pacific Bleeding Heart is extremely rare in the wild, with only one documented observation. When found, it would likely be in rich, moist woodland soils or shaded garden areas where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers partial to full shade and well-drained but consistently moist soil.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in late spring, typically May through June, with the distinctive heart-shaped blooms being the primary identifying feature during this peak season.
seasonality.summer: Flowering may continue sporadically through summer in cool, moist conditions, while the fern-like foliage remains prominent and green.
seasonality.fall: Foliage may yellow and begin to die back, with seed pods splitting to release seeds if flowers were successfully pollinated.
seasonality.winter: Plant goes dormant with all above-ground parts dying back, leaving only underground rhizomes that will sprout new growth in spring.

funFact: Pacific Bleeding Heart contains alkaloids that make it toxic to most animals, but indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest traditionally used small amounts medicinally - though this should never be attempted without expert knowledge, as the dosage between medicine and poison is extremely narrow.
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with Fringed Bleeding Heart, but Pacific Bleeding Heart has more finely divided, blue-green leaves (versus Fringed's more grayish-green, less divided foliage) and flowers that are typically more pink or purple rather than the deeper rose-red of Fringed Bleeding Heart.
contextualKnowledge: While called Pacific Bleeding Heart, this plant is essentially a garden escapee in New England - it's not part of our native flora. Gardeners sometimes grow it as an ornamental, and very rarely it may self-seed in suitable woodland conditions, which explains its single documented wild occurrence in our region.
compareHints: Pacific Bleeding Heart differs from its New England relatives by blooming later and longer than the early spring ephemerals Dutchman's Breeches and Squirrel Corn, which go dormant by early summer. Unlike these spring ephemerals, Pacific Bleeding Heart maintains its foliage through the growing season and has more finely divided, blue-green leaves compared to Fringed Bleeding Heart's grayer foliage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to squirrel corn, Dutchman's breeches has more distinctly "pantaloon-shaped" flowers with pointed spurs versus squirrel corn's heart-shaped blooms with rounded spurs.

Squirrel corn differs from Dutchman's breeches primarily in flower shape - squirrel corn has heart-shaped flowers with rounded spurs, while Dutchman's breeches has pantaloon-shaped flowers with pointed spurs.

Fringed bleeding heart differs from its cousins Dutchman's breeches and squirrel corn by blooming throughout the growing season rather than just early spring, and by its pink heart-shaped flowers instead of white pantaloon or kernel-shaped blooms.
